cards.title: Accops Powered VDI vs Citrix and VMware Horizon: Feature Comparison
cards.key_problem: A prospect evaluating Accops against Citrix DaaS/CVAD or VMware Horizon needs a line-by-line answer on where each product actually differs, rather than three vendors all claiming the same capabilities.
key_outcomes: Single-slide matrix across 24 capabilities, three vendors
Marks Citrix zero-trust gateway and MFA as 'Buy Netscaler'
Marks VMware Horizon 'Partial ($)' on most security controls
Biometric MFA: Accops Yes, both competitors Partial
Accops-only: hardened thin-client OS, thin-client supply, flexible licensing
cards.brief: A one-slide capability matrix comparing Accops Powered VDI against Citrix DaaS/CVAD and VMware Horizon across user experience, endpoint controls, data security, network security, deployment and procurement. The recurring argument is bundling: capabilities Accops includes are add-on purchases for Citrix (Netscaler for the zero-trust gateway and MFA, an add-on licence for screen-capture blocking) and mostly 'Partial ($)' for Horizon. Accops-exclusive rows are biometric MFA, DNS-based URL whitelisting on the endpoint, hardened thin-client OS, thin-client supply, and perpetual as well as subscription licensing.
cards.use_for: A live Citrix or VMware displacement deal where the prospect wants a feature-by-feature comparison. Internal reference for the rep - do not forward.
cards.internal_reason: Competitive positioning against named vendors. The PDF twin carries the same content and is footer-stamped 'Confidential Document'.

cards.title: Accops Powered VDI vs Citrix VDI: Feature Comparison
cards.key_problem: A prospect comparing Accops with Citrix DaaS/CVAD needs the differences stated capability by capability, particularly which Citrix features require buying Netscaler or an add-on licence on top.
key_outcomes: Two-vendor matrix over 24 capabilities, Accops vs Citrix only
Zero-trust gateway, token MFA and reverse proxy all 'Buy Netscaler'
Screen-capture and screen-sharing blocking need a Citrix add-on licence
Citrix marked No on biometric MFA, DNS URL whitelisting, hardened OS, thin clients
Accops cites India-based leadership, development and support as a differentiator
cards.brief: The Citrix-only cut of the comparison matrix, and the cleaner artefact for a deal where VMware is not in play. Twenty-four capabilities across user experience, endpoint control, data security, network security, deployment and procurement. Citrix matches Accops on core VDI delivery; the gaps it records are biometric MFA, DNS-based URL whitelisting, a hardened endpoint OS for refurbishing legacy PCs, thin-client supply, and remote control beyond the VDI session. Several Citrix 'Yes' entries are qualified as requiring Netscaler or a separately purchased add-on.
cards.use_for: A Citrix displacement or renewal-pressure conversation. Internal - the document is marked Confidential.
cards.internal_reason: Footer on every page reads 'Confidential Document | (c) 2024 Accops - All Rights Reserved'.

cards.title: Accops Powered VDI vs the Field: Tier 1, Public Cloud and Tier 2 Providers
cards.key_problem: A prospect running a broad VDI evaluation is comparing Accops not just with Citrix and VMware but with Azure Virtual Desktop, AWS WorkSpaces and second-tier DaaS providers, each of which wins on a different axis.
key_outcomes: Widest competitive coverage in the library: seven competitors over three matrices
Tier 1 slide: Citrix and VMware Horizon
Public cloud slide: AVD and AWS WorkSpaces
Tier 2 slide: Workspot, Parallels RAS, dinCloud
Records AVD advanced MFA and conditional access as requiring Azure AD P1/P2
cards.brief: Three comparison matrices in one deck, which makes it the broadest competitive asset in the library. The first repeats the Tier 1 Citrix and VMware comparison. The second sets Accops against Azure Virtual Desktop and AWS WorkSpaces, where the argument is licence dependency - AVD needs Azure AD P1/P2 for self-service password reset, advanced MFA and conditional access, and WorkSpaces is marked No on almost every endpoint and data-security control. The third covers Workspot, Parallels RAS and dinCloud, noting dinCloud delivers most capabilities only through Citrix or RDS underneath.
cards.use_for: An open VDI evaluation with several vendors shortlisted, especially one involving AVD or AWS. Check the content date before sending anything from it.
cards.stale_risk: The filename says 2026-06-11 but the deck is dated 29 NOV 2022 on slide 1 and every slide is stamped (c) 2022. The filename date is a SharePoint touch, not the content date - competitor capabilities have moved on since, particularly AVD. Treat as a 2022 document and verify before a live deal.

cards.title: Migration Strategy from VMware EUC: Three Full-Stack Replacement Options
cards.client: A named reference list spanning Indian banking, telecom, pharma, manufacturing, government and education, plus Japanese municipalities and universities
cards.client_actual: Axis Bank, IDFC Bank, Kotak Securities, LIC MF, Hero Fincorp, Canara Bank, HDFC Bank, Karnataka Bank, Axis Bank AMC, Motilal Oswal, Jio, Sheela Foam, Bharti AXA, Malayala Manorama, Barbeque Nation, Wockhardt Pharma, Sharda Hospital, Mphasis, DTDC, NIC, DishTV, Flipkart, Myntra, Railtel, Samsung, Zensar, Raychem, Future Generali, Jazeera Airlines, Indian Air Force, DRDO, Kyoto University, Aomori Prefectural Government
cards.key_problem: Broadcom's acquisition changed VMware's pricing, partner model and roadmap, and Horizon View runs only on vSphere - so a customer replacing vSphere or vSAN must replace Horizon at the same time, whether or not that was the plan.
key_outcomes: Three replacement stacks: Accops with Nutanix AHV, Hyper-V/SCVMM, or RedHat OpenStack
Component-by-component mapping from each VMware product to its Accops equivalent
Architecture diagram per option
Shared desktops costed at 75% cheaper than personal Windows 10/11 desktops
Scale evidence: 250,000 clientless ZTNA users, 100,000-user Azure deployment
cards.brief: The migration story for a customer leaving VMware EUC. It opens with what changed after Broadcom - price rises, a cut channel, dropped OEM relationships, and Horizon View divested to KKR - then makes the structural argument that Horizon runs only on vSphere, so replacing the hypervisor forces replacing the VDI broker too. Three full-stack options follow, each with an architecture diagram: Accops with Nutanix, with Hyper-V and SCVMM, or with RedHat OpenStack. A component table maps every VMware piece to its Accops or partner equivalent. The back half is the standard Accops platform pitch with an extensive named-customer reference list.
cards.use_for: A VMware or Horizon customer reacting to Broadcom pricing or the KKR divestiture. Internal only - the reference list names dozens of customers.
cards.internal_reason: Names dozens of real customers with deployment sizes and use cases, including banks and defence. A prospect must never see another customer's name and user count.

cards.title: Omnissa Horizon with VMware vSphere Foundation for VDI: Analysis of the Bundled Offering
cards.key_problem: Omnissa's Horizon plus VVF for VDI bundle looks cheaper as a single SKU, but the vSphere licence underneath is Broadcom's, restricted to Horizon workloads only, version-locked to vSphere 8.0 U3, and capped at a trial slice of vSAN capacity.
key_outcomes: vSAN entitlement is only 100 GiB per CPU core, a trial slice not production storage
Worked example: 20 servers x 32 cores caps the cluster at 64 TiB raw
Storage, not CPU, becomes the ceiling on scaling Horizon
vSphere Enterprise Plus licensed per user, not per core, breaking standardisation
Upgrade to vSphere 9.x explicitly not supported; keys come from Broadcom, not Omnissa
cards.brief: A structured teardown of the Omnissa Horizon plus VVF for VDI combined offering, argued from Omnissa's own FAQ (KB 6000381). Fifteen findings: the licence is legally usable only for Horizon VDI workloads so consolidation benefits disappear; vSphere is licensed per user rather than per core; Broadcom owns and fulfils the software while Omnissa merely resells it, splitting support across two vendors; the entitlement is version-locked at vSphere 8.0 U3 with 9.x unsupported; and the bundled vSAN is 100 GiB per core, which the paper's own arithmetic shows becomes the binding constraint well before CPU capacity does. Concludes with the Accops alternative: hypervisor-agnostic, flexible licensing, integrated security, local support.
cards.use_for: A prospect being offered the Omnissa bundle who believes it is the cheaper option. The vSAN capacity arithmetic is the strongest single argument in it.
cards.internal_reason: Adversarial analysis of a named competitor's licensing. Carries its own trademark disclaimer, but is written for internal enablement rather than distribution.

cards.source: sharepoint/Accops HySecure vs Zscaler Private Access v 3.3.pptx
cards.title: Accops HySecure vs Zscaler Private Access: Architecture and Feature Comparison
cards.key_problem: Zscaler Private Access routes all traffic through Zscaler's own data centres before it reaches the customer's applications, which is a data-residency and latency problem that a feature list alone does not surface.
key_outcomes: Data path is the headline difference: customer DC vs always via Zscaler DCs
Zscaler has no built-in MFA - requires an external IDP such as Azure AD
ZPA cannot do agentless RDP, VNC or VDI access; Accops can
No ZPA equivalent for endpoint DLP: print-screen, screen-share blocking, watermark
ZPA supports only always-on policies, unsuited to BYOD and contractor access
cards.brief: An architecture-led comparison rather than a feature grid alone. It draws both data paths first: with ZPA every session traverses Zscaler's cloud before entering the customer's data centre, while HySecure has the user connect to the customer's own gateway; an alternative slide covers HySecure hosted as a service. Three feature matrices follow across deployment, access control and endpoint control. The consistent gaps recorded against ZPA are built-in MFA, SAML IDP behaviour, agentless access to non-web protocols, VDI-based sandboxing, and endpoint data-leakage controls, where Zscaler's answer is network-level DLP instead. Accops is marked behind on internet and web filtering and on auto-upgrade, which is listed as upcoming.
cards.use_for: A ZTNA evaluation where Zscaler is the incumbent or the front-runner, especially where data residency or BYOD contractor access is in scope.
cards.stale_risk: No date appears anywhere in the deck; the filename carries version 3.3. Several rows are marked 'upcoming feature', so those claims need checking against the current release before use.
cards.internal_reason: Competitive positioning against a named vendor, including where Accops is behind.

cards.title: Accops HySecure vs Cisco AnyConnect and Other VPNs
cards.key_problem: A customer with a working VPN asks why they should replace it, and the honest answer is not throughput but what a VPN cannot do: contextual access, endpoint control, built-in MFA and agentless access for unmanaged devices.
key_outcomes: Protocol-level comparison: TLS 1.2 and ChaChaPoly over Noise vs IPsec
Cisco DUO licensed per named user; HySecure Gold MFA licensed on concurrency
Roughly 70% MFA cost saving claimed from concurrent rather than named licensing
Cisco VPN cannot connect to multiple data centres at once; HySecure can
Hardware-only appliance for Cisco vs deploy-anywhere virtual for HySecure
cards.brief: The answer to the 'why not just keep the VPN' objection, built mainly around Cisco AnyConnect and extending to other VPN vendors. It compares at protocol level first - transport, firewall traversal, VOIP and application support - then moves to access methods, where the argument is that a VPN offers L3 tunnelling and limited clientless access while HySecure adds L4 tunnelling and full reverse-proxy support for all applications. Deployment favours HySecure on simplicity: a single node, a single IP, no virtual IP pool, virtual or hardware. The commercial argument is licensing, with Cisco DUO priced per named user against HySecure's concurrency-based MFA.
cards.use_for: A prospect with an incumbent VPN at renewal, or one who says a VPN plus separate MFA already covers remote access.
cards.stale_risk: No date in the deck. Competitor licensing terms in particular go out of date quickly - verify the DUO comparison before quoting the 70% figure to a customer.
cards.internal_reason: Competitive positioning with specific claims about a named competitor's licensing costs.

cards.title: Accops and Forcepoint: One Workspace, Zero Trust Everywhere (Webinar Deck)
cards.key_problem: Employees are already feeding corporate data into public AI tools and AI agents now act on files and clipboards directly, so data is leaving the organisation through a path that existing controls were never designed to see.
key_outcomes: 57% of employees have entered confidential company data into public AI tools
23% of organisations have deployed AI agent-building platforms
$4.63M average cost of a breach involving shadow AI, $670K above a standard breach
Joint Accops and Forcepoint proposition: the Secure Workspace Alliance
Presented by Accops CEO Vijender Yadav with Forcepoint's Area VP for India, ANZ and SA
cards.brief: A joint webinar deck with Forcepoint, positioning a combined workspace-plus-data-security proposition around shadow AI as the current data-loss vector. It opens with Forcepoint's 2026 research - a majority of employees pasting confidential data into public AI tools, agent platforms already deployed in a quarter of organisations, and a measurably higher breach cost where shadow AI is involved - then sets out the alliance: Accops for the secure workspace and access layer, Forcepoint for data security. Partner-branded rather than a standalone Accops asset.
cards.use_for: A partner or alliance conversation, or a CISO raising shadow AI and data loss to public AI tools. The three research statistics are the reusable part.
cards.internal_reason: Co-branded partner material carrying Forcepoint's copyright and research. Not Accops' to distribute unilaterally.
